Drawing context trees and models

Source: vignettes/articles/drawing.Rmd
drawing.Rmd
library(mixvlmc)

This article describes how to represent context trees, variable length Markov chains (VLMC) and VLMC with covariates as trees, using the draw() function. draw() produces either an “ascii art” representation, well suited to the R console, or a LaTeX representation of the tree, to be included in a LaTeX document or in an R Markdown or Quarto document that produces a PDF.

draw() is a generic function with methods for the three types of objects: draw.ctx_tree() for context trees, draw.vlmc() for VLMC and draw.covlmc() for VLMC with covariates. Context trees and VLMC are drawn in the same way whatever their backend (the default C++ backend or the R one, see ctx_tree() and vlmc()). All the methods share the same organisation:

  • the format argument (the second one) selects the output format, either "text" (the default) or "latex";
  • additional arguments specific to each method specify what information is shown in each node of the tree (frequencies, probabilities, models, etc.);
  • the control argument, built with draw_control(), specifies how this information is shown (characters used to draw the tree, number of significant digits, LaTeX layout, etc.).

The methods report an error when they are given an argument they do not use, for instance an option of draw_control() given directly to draw().

This organisation of the arguments was introduced in mixvlmc 0.3.0. Calls written for previous versions, in which the second argument of draw() was the control list, still work but trigger a deprecation warning.

The models used in this article are kept very simple: see vignette("context-trees"), vignette("variable-length-markov-chains") and vignette("covlmc") for the construction and the interpretation of context trees and models.

Context trees

Basic representation

We use a small random sequence on three states.

set.seed(0)
x <- sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 100, replace = TRUE)
x_ctx <- ctx_tree(x, min_size = 10, max_depth = 2)
draw(x_ctx)
#> ▪
#> ├─ a
#> │  ├─ a
#> │  └─ b
#> ├─ b
#> │  ├─ b
#> │  └─ c
#> └─ c
#>    └─ a

The root of the tree (the empty context) is shown by a small square. Each node of the first level corresponds to the most recent state of a context (\(x_{t-1}\)), each node of the second level to the state before it (\(x_{t-2}\)), etc. A context is therefore read from its node to the root in chronological order. For instance, the leaf b under the node a stands for the context in which b is followed by a, denoted b, a by contexts():

contexts(x_ctx)
#> Contexts:
#>  a, a
#>  b, a
#>  a
#>  b, b
#>  c, b
#>  b
#>  a, c
#>  c

Frequencies

The frequency argument of draw.ctx_tree() adds the frequencies of the (partial) contexts to the representation. With frequency = "total", each node shows the number of occurrences of its context in the sequence (only the occurrences followed by at least one state are taken into account, see vignette("context-trees")).

draw(x_ctx, frequency = "total")
#> ▪ (100)
#> ├─ a (32)
#> │  ├─ a (15)
#> │  └─ b (10)
#> ├─ b (38)
#> │  ├─ b (19)
#> │  └─ c (12)
#> └─ c (29)
#>    └─ a (11)

With frequency = "detailed", each node shows the number of occurrences of each state that follows its context, in the order of the state space given by states() (here a, b, c).

draw(x_ctx, frequency = "detailed")
#> ▪ (32, 38, 30)
#> ├─ a (15, 6, 11)
#> │  ├─ a (7, 4, 4)
#> │  └─ b (4, 1, 5)
#> ├─ b (10, 19, 9)
#> │  ├─ b (3, 10, 6)
#> │  └─ c (3, 6, 3)
#> └─ c (7, 12, 10)
#>    └─ a (3, 5, 3)

This is the same information as the one given by contexts() with the same frequency argument, organised as a tree.

Variable length Markov chains

Probabilities and frequencies

Each context of a VLMC is associated with a conditional distribution of the next state. draw.vlmc() shows those distributions by default. We use as an example a VLMC fitted to a discretised version of the active power of week 5 of the household electricity consumption data set (powerconsumption). The model is selected with the BIC (see vignette("variable-length-markov-chains") and vignette("model-selection")).

pc_week_5 <- powerconsumption[powerconsumption$week == 5, ]
elec_dts <- cut(pc_week_5$active_power,
  breaks = c(0, 0.4, 2, 8),
  labels = c("low", "typical", "high")
)
elec_vlmc <- as_vlmc(tune_vlmc(elec_dts))
draw(elec_vlmc)
#> ▪ (0.1667, 0.5496, 0.2837)
#> ├─ low (0.7665, 0.2335, 0)
#> ├─ typical (0.0704, 0.8466, 0.08303)
#> │  └─ low (0.3846, 0.5385, 0.07692)
#> └─ high (0.003497, 0.1573, 0.8392)

The probabilities are given in the order of the state space, here:

states(elec_vlmc)
#> [1] low     typical high   
#> Levels: low typical high

The root node gives the marginal distribution of the states in the sequence, while the other nodes give the distribution of the next state conditionally on their (partial) context.

The prob argument controls this display: prob = FALSE replaces the probabilities by the frequencies of the states that follow each (partial) context (as frequency = "detailed" in draw.ctx_tree()), while prob = NULL removes all the information.

draw(elec_vlmc, prob = FALSE)
#> ▪ (168, 554, 286)
#> ├─ low (128, 39, 0)
#> ├─ typical (39, 469, 46)
#> │  └─ low (15, 21, 3)
#> └─ high (1, 45, 240)
draw(elec_vlmc, prob = NULL)
#> ▪
#> ├─ low
#> ├─ typical
#> │  └─ low
#> └─ high

Number of digits

Probabilities (and other numerical values) are rounded with signif() to the number of significant digits given by the digits parameter of draw_control() (4 by default).

draw(elec_vlmc, control = draw_control(digits = 2))
#> ▪ (0.17, 0.55, 0.28)
#> ├─ low (0.77, 0.23, 0)
#> ├─ typical (0.07, 0.85, 0.083)
#> │  └─ low (0.38, 0.54, 0.077)
#> └─ high (0.0035, 0.16, 0.84)

Text representations

Character sets

The “ascii art” representation uses a collection of characters, the charset, to draw the branches of the tree and to delimit the information attached to the nodes. The package provides two charsets:

  • "utf8": the charset returned by charset_utf8(), based on UTF-8 symbols (used in this article);
  • "ascii": the charset returned by charset_ascii(), based on standard ASCII characters only.

The default charset is given by the mixvlmc.charset option. When the package is loaded, this option is set to "utf8" if the output supports UTF-8 characters (according to cli::is_utf8_output()) and to "ascii" otherwise (unless the option was already set). The charset can be changed for a single call with the charset parameter of draw_control():

draw(x_ctx, control = draw_control(charset = "ascii"))
#> *
#> +-- a
#> |   +-- a
#> |   '-- b
#> +-- b
#> |   +-- b
#> |   '-- c
#> '-- c
#>     '-- a

or for all subsequent calls by setting the option:

options(mixvlmc.charset = "ascii")
draw(x_ctx, frequency = "total")
#> * (100)
#> +-- a (32)
#> |   +-- a (15)
#> |   '-- b (10)
#> +-- b (38)
#> |   +-- b (19)
#> |   '-- c (12)
#> '-- c (29)
#>     '-- a (11)
options(mixvlmc.charset = "utf8")

Custom charsets

charset_utf8() and charset_ascii() return lists of character strings, one per element of the representation. All their arguments can be modified to obtain a custom charset, which is then given to draw_control():

str(charset_ascii())
#> List of 16
#>  $ root         : chr "*"
#>  $ first_node   : chr "+"
#>  $ next_node    : chr "+"
#>  $ final_node   : chr "'"
#>  $ vbranch      : chr "|"
#>  $ hbranch      : chr "--"
#>  $ open_ct      : chr "("
#>  $ close_ct     : chr ")"
#>  $ level_sep    : chr " ~ "
#>  $ time_sep     : chr " | "
#>  $ intercept    : chr "(I)"
#>  $ intercept_sep: chr " & "
#>  $ open_p_value : chr "<"
#>  $ close_p_value: chr ">"
#>  $ open_model   : chr "["
#>  $ close_model  : chr "]"

The first elements are used for all the trees:

  • root: the symbol of the root node;
  • first_node, next_node and final_node: the symbols that introduce the first child of a node, its intermediate children and its last child;
  • vbranch and hbranch: the vertical and horizontal parts of the branches;
  • open_ct and close_ct: the delimiters of the information attached to a node (frequencies, probabilities, models).

For instance:

my_charset <- charset_ascii(
  root = "@",
  final_node = "+",
  hbranch = "==",
  open_ct = "<",
  close_ct = ">"
)
draw(x_ctx,
  frequency = "detailed",
  control = draw_control(charset = my_charset)
)
#> @ <32, 38, 30>
#> +== a <15, 6, 11>
#> |   +== a <7, 4, 4>
#> |   +== b <4, 1, 5>
#> +== b <10, 19, 9>
#> |   +== b <3, 10, 6>
#> |   +== c <3, 6, 3>
#> +== c <7, 12, 10>
#>     +== a <3, 5, 3>

The other elements (level_sep, time_sep, intercept, intercept_sep, open_p_value, close_p_value, open_model and close_model) are used only by draw.covlmc() and are described below.

VLMC with covariates

A two-state model

A VLMC with covariates (see vignette("covlmc")) associates to each context a logistic model that gives the conditional distribution of the next state as a function of past values of the covariates. draw.covlmc() represents those models in the tree. We start with a two-state sequence and a single logical covariate.

elec_dts_2 <- cut(pc_week_5$active_power,
  breaks = c(0, median(pc_week_5$active_power), 8),
  labels = c("low", "high")
)
elec_cov <- data.frame(day = (pc_week_5$hour >= 7 & pc_week_5$hour <= 17))
elec_covlmc <- covlmc(elec_dts_2, elec_cov, min_size = 5)
draw(elec_covlmc)
#> ▪
#> ├─ low
#> │  ├─ low
#> │  │  ├─ low ([ -2.813 • 2.178 ⁞ -4.449 ⁞ 2.418 ])
#> │  │  └─ high ([ -19.57 • 18.39 ])
#> │  └─ high (0.8649, 0.1351)
#> └─ high (0.07341, 0.9266)

Two types of models appear in the tree:

  • constant models do not depend on the covariates. By default, they are represented by the conditional distribution of the next state that they induce, as for a VLMC (in the order of states(elec_covlmc));
  • other models are represented between brackets by their coefficients. With a logistic model, the coefficients describe the logarithm of the ratio between the probability of the second state (here high) and the probability of the first state (here low, the reference state). The intercept comes first, followed by the coefficients of the covariates at time \(t-1\), then at time \(t-2\), etc. The intercept is separated from the other coefficients by the intercept_sep element of the charset (a bullet with UTF-8 characters) and consecutive time steps are separated by the time_sep element (a vertical dotted line with UTF-8 characters).

For instance, the model of the context made of three consecutive low states (the deepest low leaf) has an intercept followed by one coefficient for each of the values of day at times \(t-1\), \(t-2\) and \(t-3\), while the model of its sibling high only uses the value of day at time \(t-1\).

Setting constant_as_prob = FALSE represents constant models by their coefficients, that is by their intercept only:

draw(elec_covlmc, constant_as_prob = FALSE)
#> ▪
#> ├─ low
#> │  ├─ low
#> │  │  ├─ low ([ -2.813 • 2.178 ⁞ -4.449 ⁞ 2.418 ])
#> │  │  └─ high ([ -19.57 • 18.39 ])
#> │  └─ high ([ -1.856 ])
#> └─ high ([ 2.535 ])

The probabilities shown in the default representation are obtained from the intercepts with the logistic function. With model = "full", the names of the variables are shown above the coefficients (and constant models are always represented by their coefficients):

draw(elec_covlmc, model = "full")
#> ▪
#> ├─ low
#> │  ├─ low
#> │  │  ├─ low ([ (I)    • day_1TRUE ⁞ day_2TRUE ⁞ day_3TRUE
#> │  │  │         -2.813 • 2.178     ⁞ -4.449    ⁞ 2.418     ])
#> │  │  └─ high ([ (I)    • day_1TRUE
#> │  │             -19.57 • 18.39     ])
#> │  └─ high ([ (I)   
#> │             -1.856 ])
#> └─ high ([ (I)  
#>            2.535 ])

The names of the variables are generated by the underlying logistic model and include the time delay: for instance day_1TRUE stands for the value TRUE of the covariate day at time \(t-1\). The intercept is denoted by the intercept element of the charset ((I) by default).

With with_state = TRUE, each row of coefficients is preceded by the state it predicts. With model = "coef" (the default), the state is followed by the reference state, while with model = "full" the reference state is shown, in parentheses, on the row of the variable names. States are separated from the coefficients by the level_sep element of the charset. Constant models represented by probabilities are not modified.

draw(elec_covlmc, with_state = TRUE)
#> ▪
#> ├─ low
#> │  ├─ low
#> │  │  ├─ low ([ high/low ~ -2.813 • 2.178 ⁞ -4.449 ⁞ 2.418 ])
#> │  │  └─ high ([ high/low ~ -19.57 • 18.39 ])
#> │  └─ high (0.8649, 0.1351)
#> └─ high (0.07341, 0.9266)
draw(elec_covlmc, model = "full", with_state = TRUE)
#> ▪
#> ├─ low
#> │  ├─ low
#> │  │  ├─ low ([ (low) ~ (I)    • day_1TRUE ⁞ day_2TRUE ⁞ day_3TRUE
#> │  │  │         high  ~ -2.813 • 2.178     ⁞ -4.449    ⁞ 2.418     ])
#> │  │  └─ high ([ (low) ~ (I)    • day_1TRUE
#> │  │             high  ~ -19.57 • 18.39     ])
#> │  └─ high ([ (low) ~ (I)   
#> │             high  ~ -1.856 ])
#> └─ high ([ (low) ~ (I)  
#>            high  ~ 2.535 ])

This option is particularly useful when some states never follow a context: they are then removed from its logistic model, which has fewer rows of coefficients than expected (see examples in vignette("covlmc") and in the article on computing engines).

More states and covariates

With more than two states, the logistic models have one row of coefficients for each state but the reference one. Moreover, each time step can be associated with several coefficients: a numerical or logical covariate has one coefficient per time step, while a factor has one coefficient per level, except the first one. We illustrate this with a simulated sequence on three states and a factor covariate with three levels.

set.seed(0)
z <- sample(c("A", "B", "C"), 1000, replace = TRUE)
y <- ifelse(runif(length(z)) > 0.5,
  c(z[-1], sample(c("A", "B", "C"), 1)),
  c(z[-c(1, 2)], sample(c("A", "B", "C"), 2, replace = TRUE))
)
y <- as.factor(ifelse(runif(length(z)) > 0.2, y,
  sample(c("A", "B", "C"), length(z), replace = TRUE)
))
z_covlmc <- covlmc(z, data.frame(y = y), min_size = 1.5, alpha = 0.01)
draw(z_covlmc, model = "full", with_state = TRUE)
#> ▪
#> ├─ A
#> │  ├─ A ([ (A) ~ (I)    • y_1B   y_1C    ⁞ y_2B   y_2C 
#> │  │       B   ~ -1.393 • 1.966  -0.2701 ⁞ 1.957  1.173
#> │  │       C   ~ -1.296 • 0.7838 1.216   ⁞ -0.942 2.738 ])
#> │  ├─ B ([ (A) ~ (I)    • y_1B  y_1C   ⁞ y_2B   y_2C 
#> │  │       B   ~ -2.428 • 2.935 0.2797 ⁞ 2.627  -15  
#> │  │       C   ~ -1.588 • 1.07  1.347  ⁞ 0.8597 3.026 ])
#> │  └─ C ([ (A) ~ (I)    • y_1B   y_1C   ⁞ y_2B     y_2C   
#> │          B   ~ -1.083 • 1.779  0.5446 ⁞ 1.275    -0.5394
#> │          C   ~ -1.469 • 0.3142 2.158  ⁞ -0.02489 2.407   ])
#> ├─ B
#> │  ├─ A ([ (A) ~ (I)    • y_1B   y_1C  ⁞ y_2B  y_2C 
#> │  │       B   ~ -3.238 • 2.005  0.938 ⁞ 2.525 2.54 
#> │  │       C   ~ -3.142 • 0.5409 2.655 ⁞ 1.66  3.751 ])
#> │  ├─ B
#> │  │  ├─ C ([ (A) ~ (I)    • y_1B  y_1C   ⁞ y_2B  y_2C  ⁞ y_3B    y_3C 
#> │  │  │       B   ~ -15.19 • 1.787 0.6895 ⁞ 15.16 6.893 ⁞ 0.04448 6.859
#> │  │  │       C   ~ -40.68 • 13.8  28.11  ⁞ 8.893 17.34 ⁞ 4.27    32.35 ])
#> │  │  └─ A, B ([ (A) ~ (I)    • y_1B  y_1C    ⁞ y_2B  y_2C 
#> │  │             B   ~ -1.903 • 2.478 -0.1105 ⁞ 1.416 1.977
#> │  │             C   ~ -3.479 • 1.097 1.725   ⁞ 2.142 4.777 ])
#> │  └─ C ([ (A) ~ (I)    • y_1B  y_1C  ⁞ y_2B  y_2C 
#> │          B   ~ -4.997 • 4.323 3.73  ⁞ 2.829 4.266
#> │          C   ~ -22.39 • 4.75  5.124 ⁞ 18.4  22.28 ])
#> └─ C
#>    ├─ A ([ (A) ~ (I)    • y_1B   y_1C  ⁞ y_2B  y_2C 
#>    │       B   ~ -3.164 • 1.954  1.545 ⁞ 4.954 2.35 
#>    │       C   ~ -2.597 • 0.9274 1.851 ⁞ 1.814 2.125 ])
#>    ├─ B ([ (A) ~ (I)    • y_1B  y_1C  ⁞ y_2B     y_2C 
#>    │       B   ~ -2.166 • 1.553 1.428 ⁞ 2.332    1.055
#>    │       C   ~ -2.165 • 1.206 2.875 ⁞ -0.07224 1.419 ])
#>    └─ C ([ (A) ~ (I)    • y_1B   y_1C   ⁞ y_2B  y_2C 
#>            B   ~ -3.412 • 0.8723 0.9043 ⁞ 5.503 2.849
#>            C   ~ -4.026 • 0.8833 2.359  ⁞ 4.067 3.186 ])

In this representation, y_1B and y_1C stand for the levels B and C of the covariate y at time \(t-1\), while y_2B and y_2C stand for the same levels at time \(t-2\), etc.

The tree also shows a merged context: the leaf labelled A, B under the node B of the second level represents the two contexts A, B, B and B, B, B (in chronological order), which share a single logistic model. The fitting algorithm of covlmc() merges contexts in this way when their models are not significantly different (see vignette("covlmc"), and vignette("dts-and-contexts") for the exploration of merged contexts).

p-values

During the construction of the model, covlmc() conducts a series of likelihood ratio tests. Their p-values are included in the representation when p_value = TRUE:

draw(z_covlmc, p_value = TRUE)
#> ▪
#> ├─ A
#> │  ├─ A (‹6.085e-09› [ -1.393 • 1.966  -0.2701 ⁞ 1.957  1.173
#> │  │                   -1.296 • 0.7838 1.216   ⁞ -0.942 2.738 ])
#> │  ├─ B (‹8.921e-10› [ -2.428 • 2.935 0.2797 ⁞ 2.627  -15  
#> │  │                   -1.588 • 1.07  1.347  ⁞ 0.8597 3.026 ])
#> │  └─ C (‹1.23e-05› [ -1.083 • 1.779  0.5446 ⁞ 1.275    -0.5394
#> │                     -1.469 • 0.3142 2.158  ⁞ -0.02489 2.407   ])
#> ├─ B
#> │  ├─ A (‹4.786e-05› [ -3.238 • 2.005  0.938 ⁞ 2.525 2.54 
#> │  │                   -3.142 • 0.5409 2.655 ⁞ 1.66  3.751 ])
#> │  ├─ B
#> │  │  ├─ C (‹0.00761› [ -15.19 • 1.787 0.6895 ⁞ 15.16 6.893 ⁞ 0.04448 6.859
#> │  │  │                 -40.68 • 13.8  28.11  ⁞ 8.893 17.34 ⁞ 4.27    32.35 ])
#> │  │  └─ A, B (‹0.000705› [ -1.903 • 2.478 -0.1105 ⁞ 1.416 1.977
#> │  │                        -3.479 • 1.097 1.725   ⁞ 2.142 4.777 ])
#> │  └─ C (‹3.541e-11› [ -4.997 • 4.323 3.73  ⁞ 2.829 4.266
#> │                      -22.39 • 4.75  5.124 ⁞ 18.4  22.28 ])
#> └─ C
#>    ├─ A (‹3.459e-09› [ -3.164 • 1.954  1.545 ⁞ 4.954 2.35 
#>    │                   -2.597 • 0.9274 1.851 ⁞ 1.814 2.125 ])
#>    ├─ B (‹0.0009756› [ -2.166 • 1.553 1.428 ⁞ 2.332    1.055
#>    │                   -2.165 • 1.206 2.875 ⁞ -0.07224 1.419 ])
#>    └─ C (‹3.65e-08› [ -3.412 • 0.8723 0.9043 ⁞ 5.503 2.849
#>                       -4.026 • 0.8833 2.359  ⁞ 4.067 3.186 ])

The p-value attached to a model, shown between the open_p_value and close_p_value delimiters of the charset, is associated with the test that compares the model to a model with a shorter memory of the covariates. Internal nodes can show p-values associated with the merging of some of their children (merging) or with the removal of all their children (collapsing), as explained in vignette("covlmc"). The models can be removed from the representation with model = NULL, which gives a compact view of the p-values:

draw(z_covlmc, model = NULL, p_value = TRUE)
#> ▪
#> ├─ A
#> │  ├─ A (6.085e-09)
#> │  ├─ B (8.921e-10)
#> │  └─ C (1.23e-05)
#> ├─ B
#> │  ├─ A (4.786e-05)
#> │  ├─ B
#> │  │  ├─ C (0.00761)
#> │  │  └─ A, B (0.000705)
#> │  └─ C (3.541e-11)
#> └─ C
#>    ├─ A (3.459e-09)
#>    ├─ B (0.0009756)
#>    └─ C (3.65e-08)

Customising the model representation

The elements of the charset dedicated to draw.covlmc() can be modified as the other ones. For instance, the following charset uses + between the intercept and the other coefficients, ; between time steps, : between the states and the coefficients, and braces around the models:

cov_charset <- charset_utf8(
  intercept_sep = " + ",
  time_sep = " ; ",
  level_sep = " : ",
  open_model = "{",
  close_model = "}"
)
draw(elec_covlmc,
  model = "full", with_state = TRUE,
  control = draw_control(charset = cov_charset, digits = 3)
)
#> ▪
#> ├─ low
#> │  ├─ low
#> │  │  ├─ low ({ (low) : (I)   + day_1TRUE ; day_2TRUE ; day_3TRUE
#> │  │  │         high  : -2.81 + 2.18      ; -4.45     ; 2.42      })
#> │  │  └─ high ({ (low) : (I)   + day_1TRUE
#> │  │             high  : -19.6 + 18.4      })
#> │  └─ high ({ (low) : (I)  
#> │             high  : -1.86 })
#> └─ high ({ (low) : (I) 
#>            high  : 2.54 })

The result of draw()

draw() does not print anything by itself: it returns an object of class mixvlmc_draw that contains the representation of the tree, one line per element.

x_draw <- draw(x_ctx)
class(x_draw)
#> [1] "mixvlmc_draw"

As for other R objects, this object is printed automatically when the result of draw() is not assigned to a variable at top level, which is why calling draw(x_ctx) in the console (or in a chunk of an R Markdown document) displays the tree. Inside a function or a loop, automatic printing does not happen and the representation must be printed explicitly with print():

for (depth in 1:2) {
  print(draw(ctx_tree(x, min_size = 10, max_depth = depth)))
}
#> ▪
#> ├─ a
#> ├─ b
#> └─ c
#> ▪
#> ├─ a
#> │  ├─ a
#> │  └─ b
#> ├─ b
#> │  ├─ b
#> │  └─ c
#> └─ c
#>    └─ a

The lines of the representation are obtained as a character vector with format() or as.character():

as.character(x_draw)
#> [1] "▪"       "├─ a"    "│  ├─ a" "│  └─ b" "├─ b"    "│  ├─ b" "│  └─ c"
#> [8] "└─ c"    "   └─ a"

They can be written to a file with writeLines(), for instance to include a LaTeX representation in a document (see below):

tree_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".tex")
writeLines(format(draw(x_ctx, "latex")), tree_file)

LaTeX representations

The forest package

With format = "latex", draw() produces LaTeX code based on the forest LaTeX package. Each call produces a complete forest environment in which each node is described between square brackets, the children of a node being nested in its description. The root of the tree is represented by \(\epsilon\) (the empty context). In this HTML article, the code is shown as standard R output:

draw(x_ctx, "latex")
#> \begin{forest}
#> [\textbf{$\epsilon$}
#> [\textbf{a}
#> [\textbf{a}]
#> [\textbf{b}]]
#> [\textbf{b}
#> [\textbf{b}]
#> [\textbf{c}]]
#> [\textbf{c}
#> [\textbf{a}]]]
#> \end{forest}

The additional arguments of the methods have the same meaning as in the text format. Node information is represented by default in a small table, with the label of the node on a first row and its frequencies, probabilities or model on the following one(s):

draw(x_ctx, "latex", frequency = "detailed")
#> \begin{forest}
#> [\multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{$\epsilon$}}\\\hline
#> {\small 32}&{\small 38}&{\small 30}, align=ccc
#> [\multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{a}}\\\hline
#> {\small 15}&{\small 6}&{\small 11}, align=ccc
#> [\multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{a}}\\\hline
#> {\small 7}&{\small 4}&{\small 4}, align=ccc]
#> [\multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{b}}\\\hline
#> {\small 4}&{\small 1}&{\small 5}, align=ccc]]
#> [\multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{b}}\\\hline
#> {\small 10}&{\small 19}&{\small 9}, align=ccc
#> [\multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{b}}\\\hline
#> {\small 3}&{\small 10}&{\small 6}, align=ccc]
#> [\multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{c}}\\\hline
#> {\small 3}&{\small 6}&{\small 3}, align=ccc]]
#> [\multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{c}}\\\hline
#> {\small 7}&{\small 12}&{\small 10}, align=ccc
#> [\multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{a}}\\\hline
#> {\small 3}&{\small 5}&{\small 3}, align=ccc]]]
#> \end{forest}

The names of the states are sanitised to avoid problems induced by LaTeX special characters:

x_special <- sample(c("$1", "a_b", "{c}"), 100, replace = TRUE)
draw(ctx_tree(x_special, max_depth = 1), "latex")
#> \begin{forest}
#> [\textbf{$\epsilon$}
#> [\textbf{\{c\}}]
#> [\textbf{\$1}]
#> [\textbf{a\_b}]]
#> \end{forest}

Customising the LaTeX output

The following parameters of draw_control() apply to the LaTeX format:

  • tabular: when FALSE, the information attached to a node is given after its label, between parentheses, instead of in a table (this parameter is ignored by draw.covlmc(), which always uses tables);
  • orientation: "vertical" (default) draws the tree from top to bottom, while "horizontal" draws it from right to left;
  • decoration: "none" (default), "rectangle", "circle" or "ellipse" adds borders of the corresponding shape around all the nodes;
  • fontsize and prob_fontsize: the LaTeX font sizes (such as "small" or "large") of the labels of the nodes and of the additional information ("normalsize" and "small" by default);
  • digits: the number of significant digits, as for the text format.
draw(elec_vlmc, "latex",
  control = draw_control(
    tabular = FALSE,
    orientation = "horizontal",
    decoration = "rectangle",
    fontsize = "small",
    prob_fontsize = "footnotesize",
    digits = 2
  )
)
#> \begin{small}
#> \begin{forest}
#>   for tree={draw, grow'=west}
#> [{\textbf{$\epsilon$} {\footnotesize (0.17,0.55,0.28)}}
#> [{\textbf{low} {\footnotesize (0.77,0.23,0)}}]
#> [{\textbf{typical} {\footnotesize (0.07,0.85,0.083)}}
#> [{\textbf{low} {\footnotesize (0.38,0.54,0.077)}}]]
#> [{\textbf{high} {\footnotesize (0.0035,0.16,0.84)}}]]
#> \end{forest}
#> \end{small}

VLMC with covariates

The LaTeX representation of a VLMC with covariates differs from its text counterpart:

  • models are always represented with the names of the variables, unless model = NULL ("coef" and "full" are equivalent);
  • constant models are always represented by the probability distribution they induce (constant_as_prob is ignored);
  • the intercept is denoted (I) and the variables are given with a temporal subscript of the form \(t-1\), \(t-2\), etc. They are named after the covariates, with the level between square brackets for a factor or a logical covariate, as in y[B] or day[TRUE];
  • the coefficients of the levels of a factor that are absent from the data of a context, which are not estimated, are represented by zeros, whatever the computing engine (in the text format, VGAM::vglm() gives no coefficient for them, see the article on computing engines);
  • p-values (with p_value = TRUE) are given in parentheses after the labels of the nodes.

The tab_orientation parameter of draw_control() specifies the layout of the tables that represent the models. By default ("vertical"), the variables are listed in the first column, followed by one column of coefficients per non-reference state, which is well adapted to models with a long memory of the covariates. With with_state = TRUE, the first row gives the reference state (above the variables) and the other states (above their coefficients):

draw(elec_covlmc, "latex", with_state = TRUE)
#> \begin{forest}
#> [\textbf{$\epsilon$}
#> [\textbf{low}
#> [\textbf{low}
#> [\multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{low}}\\\hline
#> {\small low}&\textbf{{\small high}}\\{\small (I)}&{\small -2.813}\\
#> {\small $\text{day[TRUE]}_{t-1}$}&{\small 2.178}\\
#> {\small $\text{day[TRUE]}_{t-2}$}&{\small -4.449}\\
#> {\small $\text{day[TRUE]}_{t-3}$}&{\small 2.418}\\, align=cc]
#> [\multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{high}}\\\hline
#> {\small low}&\textbf{{\small high}}\\{\small (I)}&{\small -19.57}\\
#> {\small $\text{day[TRUE]}_{t-1}$}&{\small 18.39}\\, align=cc]]
#> [\multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{high}}\\\hline
#> {\small 0.8649}&{\small 0.1351}, align=cc]]
#> [\multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{high}}\\\hline
#> {\small 0.07341}&{\small 0.9266}, align=cc]]
#> \end{forest}

With tab_orientation = "horizontal", the variables are listed in the first row, followed by one row of coefficients per non-reference state (the reference state and the other states are then given in the first column when with_state = TRUE):

draw(elec_covlmc, "latex",
  with_state = TRUE,
  control = draw_control(tab_orientation = "horizontal")
)
#> \begin{forest}
#> [\textbf{$\epsilon$}
#> [\textbf{low}
#> [\textbf{low}
#> [\multicolumn{5}{c}{\textbf{low}}\\\hline
#> {\small low}&{\small (I)}&{\small $\text{day[TRUE]}_{t-1}$}&{\small $\text{day[TRUE]}_{t-2}$}&{\small $\text{day[TRUE]}_{t-3}$}\\
#> \textbf{{\small high}}&{\small -2.813}&{\small 2.178}&{\small -4.449}&{\small 2.418}, align=ccccc]
#> [\multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{high}}\\\hline
#> {\small low}&{\small (I)}&{\small $\text{day[TRUE]}_{t-1}$}\\
#> \textbf{{\small high}}&{\small -19.57}&{\small 18.39}, align=ccc]]
#> [\multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{high}}\\\hline
#> {\small 0.8649}&{\small 0.1351}, align=cc]]
#> [\multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{high}}\\\hline
#> {\small 0.07341}&{\small 0.9266}, align=cc]]
#> \end{forest}

With three states or more, the tables have several columns (or rows) of coefficients, as illustrated below with a simpler version of the three-state model used above, whose contexts are limited to a length of one:

z_covlmc_1 <- covlmc(z, data.frame(y = y),
  min_size = 1.5, alpha = 0.01, max_depth = 1
)
draw(z_covlmc_1, "latex", with_state = TRUE)
#> \begin{forest}
#> [\textbf{$\epsilon$}
#> [\multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{A}}\\\hline
#> {\small A}&\textbf{{\small B}}&\textbf{{\small C}}\\{\small (I)}&{\small -1.099}&{\small -0.8755}\\
#> {\small $\text{y[B]}_{t-1}$}&{\small 2.227}&{\small 0.9199}\\
#> {\small $\text{y[C]}_{t-1}$}&{\small 0.3102}&{\small 1.598}\\
#> , align=ccc]
#> [\multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{B}}\\\hline
#> {\small A}&\textbf{{\small B}}&\textbf{{\small C}}\\{\small (I)}&{\small -1.346}&{\small -1.806}\\
#> {\small $\text{y[B]}_{t-1}$}&{\small 2.432}&{\small 1.554}\\
#> {\small $\text{y[C]}_{t-1}$}&{\small 1.346}&{\small 2.775}\\
#> , align=ccc]
#> [\multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{C}}\\\hline
#> {\small A}&\textbf{{\small B}}&\textbf{{\small C}}\\{\small (I)}&{\small -0.8755}&{\small -1.15}\\
#> {\small $\text{y[B]}_{t-1}$}&{\small 1.569}&{\small 0.7985}\\
#> {\small $\text{y[C]}_{t-1}$}&{\small 1.227}&{\small 2.3}\\
#> , align=ccc]]
#> \end{forest}

Using the LaTeX code

In a LaTeX document, the code produced by draw() can be included as is (for instance with \input{} applied to a file obtained with writeLines(), as shown above), provided the forest package is loaded in the preamble of the document:

\usepackage{forest}

In an R Markdown or Quarto document that produces LaTeX (for instance a PDF document), no specific step is needed: calling draw(model, "latex") in a chunk is enough to render the tree. Indeed, when the output of the document is LaTeX, the LaTeX representation is included as is in the document, without the need for a results = "asis" chunk option, and the forest package is added automatically to the preamble. More precisely, the package adds the following lines to the preamble:

\usepackage{etoolbox}
\AtEndPreamble{\csname @ifpackageloaded\endcsname{forest}{}{\usepackage{forest}}}

The \AtEndPreamble command of the etoolbox package delays the loading of forest to the end of the preamble, where it is loaded only if the document has not loaded it already. A document can therefore load forest itself, anywhere in its preamble and possibly with options (such as \usepackage[external]{forest}, to cache the trees), without conflict.

Each tree is included as a paragraph of its own: when a chunk draws several trees, they are placed one below the other.

In other output formats, such as the HTML format of this article, the LaTeX representation is shown as standard R output. Finally, notice that text representations remain available in a document that produces LaTeX. As the mixvlmc.charset option is set when the package is loaded, it is set to "ascii" when the package is loaded while knitting such a document (cli::is_utf8_output() reports that LaTeX output does not support UTF-8 characters).
